title: Camp 4 close: the thirtieth part
hookLine: the part every Muslim child knows is now yours too

lines: A CHILD ON A MOSQUE CARPET.
cards: Somewhere right now, a seven-year-old is sitting cross-legged on a mosque carpet, rocking slightly, reciting Qul a'udhu bi rabbin-nas for the hundredth time while a teacher listens with one ear and corrects with one finger.
Tomorrow it'll be the next surah. In a few years, the whole last part. It's the same in Karachi, Lagos, Istanbul, Detroit.
The children don't start with the long surahs at the front of the book. They start at the end, with the short ones, and work backward. That's exactly what you've done for seventy-five days.

teach.b: Look back at the road. You began by hearing before reading: tilawah, the Qur'an as something recited aloud before it was ever a book on a shelf. Then ta'awwudh, taking refuge before you begin.
Then An-Nas, the whisperer who withdraws, and from there backward, surah by surah. Al-Ikhlas and the One, ahad. Al-Kawthar's abundance.
Al-Ma'un's small kindnesses. By time, people are in loss. The earth telling its news.
Al-Qadr, peace until dawn. Read, the first word ever revealed. With hardship, ease.
The orphan, again and again. The soul at peace, returning. Al-Wadud, the Loving.
The buried girl who will be asked. The man who frowned, and was corrected. Until An-Naba', the great news, where the juz' begins.

teach.h: CARRIED INTO PRAYER, SLEEP AND VOICE.
teach.b: Then you carried it: into prayer, into sleep with Ayat al-Kursi, into the Fatiha heard fresh, into tajwid and zayyinu, into one verse, kept.

Bukhari records the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ saying: the best of you are those who learn the Qur'an and teach it. That's why the seven-year-old is on the carpet, and why a grandparent somewhere is listening.
The juz' isn't the whole Qur'an.

teach.h: THE DOORWAY MOST PEOPLE WALK THROUGH.
teach.b: It's the doorway most people walk through.

Now the path goes further in. Camp five has four strands: the most beautiful names of Allah, the Prophet's life in Medina, Rumi and the Sufi path for those who choose it, and how the Qur'an itself is built.

how: Muslim children usually memorize Juz' 'Amma first, from An-Nas backward, with a teacher at a mosque, a weekend school or at home; in many families finishing it is marked with a small celebration.

o: copying the Qur'an out by hand

games.q: the camp's road — tap the pairs.

s: children usually learn the Qur'an starting from Surah 2
most start at the end, with Juz' 'Amma, and work backward.
the Prophet said the best are those who learn the Qur'an and teach it
Juz' 'Amma is the whole of what Muslims memorize
it's the doorway: one part of thirty.

games.q: the Prophet names who is best among you. who?
o: those who learn the Qur'an and teach it
those who read the most pages
games.why: Bukhari: the best of you are those who learn the Qur'an and teach it. the child and the teacher both count.

practice: Sit the way that child sits, if your body lets you, and choose one surah you know by heart, or nearly: al-Ikhlas is four lines, the Fatiha seven, and if you don't have a whole one yet, take the verse you kept yesterday.
Recite it from memory, without looking, slowly, in Arabic or in English, and if you stumble, remember the two rewards and keep going. When you finish, sit in the quiet: this is in you now.

wordCard.voice: Hifz, keeping and memorizing: seventy-five days through the thirtieth part, from An-Nas back to An-Naba', the surahs every Muslim child learns first.

orig.note: Arabic: keeping, memorizing. one who memorizes the whole Qur'an is a hafiz.

carryVoice: Your line: the ones every child knows. Now they're yours too. Camp four, complete.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 5027 (the best of you learn the Qur'an and teach it)
Sahih al-Bukhari 4937; Sahih Muslim 798 (two rewards for the one who finds it hard)
